opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most fundamental problems, and in some ways it's more fundamental than the problems we usually associate with intelligence. There's this old observation, sometimes called Moravec's paradox, that the things we think of as hard, like playing chess or proving theorems, turned out to be relatively easy for computers. The things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a toy, walking across a cluttered room, or stacking blocks, turned out to be extraordinarily hard.

If you look at evolution, that makes sense. Life on Earth has been around for something like three and a half billion years. Nervous systems that couple perception and action have been evolving for over five hundred million years. Language and abstract reasoning are very recent, maybe a few hundred thousand years at most. So most of the "intelligence" in the biological sense went into sensorimotor control: seeing, moving, manipulating, getting around in the world. That is the foundation everything else is built on.

So as a research agenda, I think of it in a few ways. First, perception and action have to be studied together. For a long time in computer vision we treated vision as passive. You take an image, you label it, you segment it. But biological vision evolved to guide action. A frog's vision is there to catch flies. When you put perception in the service of action, the problems change. You care about affordances, about what you can grasp, where you can step, not just what category something belongs to.

Second, learning has to play a central role. Classical robotics had a lot of beautiful work on modeling and control, and that matters. But the real world is too varied to hand-engineer everything. Children learn through enormous amounts of play and exploration and trial and error. Babies flail around, they put things in their mouths, they drop things repeatedly. That isn't wasted time. It is how they build models of their bodies and of the physical world. I think robots need something analogous: lots of experience, whether in simulation, in the real world, or ideally both.

That ties into some of the work we've done on legged locomotion, for example. We trained policies in simulation with a lot of variation in terrain, friction, and dynamics, and then deployed them on real robots. The key was that the robot could adapt online. It would infer something about the conditions it was in, a slippery floor or soft ground or a heavy payload, and adjust its behavior within a fraction of a second. That kind of rapid motor adaptation is something animals do all the time, and it is essential if you want robots to work outside carefully controlled settings.

Third, I'd say we should take inspiration from developmental psychology. There's a lovely progression in children: they first gain control over their own bodies, then they learn to reach and grasp, then to manipulate objects with intent, then to use tools. Language comes in along the way and ties into all of this. I find that progression a useful guide for thinking about curricula for robots.

So my view is that sensorimotor skill acquisition isn't a niche corner of AI. In many ways it is the core. If we can get robots to learn to see, move, and manipulate with the flexibility of even a young child, a lot of what we call higher cognition will have a much firmer foundation to build on.

r001.rationale: The response gives a developmental progression from body control to reaching, grasping, manipulation, and tool use, but does not describe complex skills as compositions of simpler skills.

r002.rationale: It discusses children learning through play and exploration, but does not explain that apparently rapid learning of a complex task can depend on skills acquired over many prior years.

r003.rationale: It calls developmental progression a useful guide for robot curricula, but does not identify making later robot skill acquisition more efficient through prior skill acquisition as a research goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the right starting point is to notice that we've been going at this a bit backwards for a long time. If you look at the history of AI, the early work was obsessed with what you might call the hallmarks of human intelligence — playing chess, proving theorems, doing symbolic reasoning. And those turned out to be, in a sense, the easy problems. The hard problems are the ones a two-year-old solves effortlessly: picking up a cup, walking across a cluttered room, looking at a scene and understanding what's there. This is Moravec's paradox, and it's held up remarkably well.

So when I think about sensorimotor skill acquisition, I think about it as the foundation rather than a peripheral application. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years on perception and motor control, and only a very short time on language and abstract thought. That tells you something about where the difficulty lies, and it also suggests that the abstract capabilities are built on top of the sensorimotor ones, not independent of them.

Now, how do you actually do the research? My view is that you want to take inspiration from development without being slavish about it. A human infant isn't given a reward function and a million trials. The child explores, plays, has a body that constrains what's possible, and has a caregiver who provides a bit of scaffolding. There's a progression — first you learn to control your body, then you learn to manipulate objects, then you start to understand the physical and social world through those interactions. I think that ordering matters, and I think it's a mistake to try to learn everything in one undifferentiated end-to-end blob.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this agenda forces honesty. In vision we got a lot of mileage from large labeled datasets, and that's fine, but it can also let you fool yourself about what the system actually understands. When you have to close the loop — perceive, act, see the consequence — the world pushes back. You can't fake grasping a cup. So I see robotics not just as an application of perception, but as the ultimate test of it. If our understanding of vision is right, we should be able to build a machine that uses it to do something in the world.

Practically, that means a few bets. Simulation is going to be essential for the amount of experience needed — you simply can't collect enough real data otherwise, so sim-to-real transfer is a core problem, not a hack. Legged locomotion has been a nice domain for this because the dynamics are hard but the perception requirements are tractable, and we've seen reinforcement learning in simulation produce controllers that work on real robots in quite rough terrain. Manipulation is the harder frontier, because the contact dynamics are messy and the perceptual demands are far greater. That's where I think the field will be spending the next decade.

And I'd say we should be patient. The goal isn't a robot that does one impressive demo. It's a robot that acquires skills the way a child does — incrementally, from its own experience, building a repertoire that generalizes. If we get that, I think we'll also have learned something deep about intelligence itself.

r001.rationale: It gives a developmental progression from body control to object manipulation and understanding the world, but does not describe complex skills as compositions of simpler skills.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that apparently rapid learning of a complex task can depend on skills acquired over many prior years.

r003.rationale: It advocates incremental skill acquisition and building a repertoire, but does not identify making later skill acquisition more efficient through earlier skills as a research goal.

astra-6.text:
I think sensorimotor skill acquisition is one of the central problems in robotics. We tend to focus on the things humans find intellectually difficult, but the things we do almost without thinking—picking up an object, putting on a shirt, walking across an unfamiliar surface—are extraordinarily demanding for a robot.

And these are not purely perception problems or purely control problems. You see something, you act, the action changes what you see and what you feel, and you adjust. So the research agenda has to address that whole loop. How does a robot learn from its own interaction with the world? How does experience with one object help it handle another? How does it recover when its initial action doesn't work?

I would distinguish learning a particular task from acquiring a skill. You can engineer a system to repeat a movement in a very controlled setting. But a useful skill has some range: it works when the object moves, when the geometry changes, when the conditions are a little different. Understanding how to acquire that flexibility, and how to build more complex behavior from those skills, is a very substantial research agenda.

r001.rationale: It says complex behavior can be built from acquired skills, which conveys combining simpler skills into more complex behavior.

r002.rationale: It describes everyday tasks as demanding for robots, but does not say humans’ apparent rapid learning relies on skills acquired over many prior years.

r003.rationale: It asks how experience with one object might help with another, but does not identify making later robot skill acquisition more efficient as a research goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think sensorimotor skill acquisition is one of the central problems in robotics. It is very easy to underestimate how much intelligence is involved in ordinary physical behavior. A child can pick up an unfamiliar object, turn it around, and figure out how to use it. For a robot, each part of that is still a substantial challenge.

The important thing is to study perception and action together. You don't just look at the world, construct a complete description, and then act. You act to learn something about the world. If you are uncertain about an object, you might touch it or move it, and that gives you information that vision alone doesn't provide.

So the research agenda, to me, is about learning reusable skills through interaction. How do you acquire a skill, how do you improve it with experience, and how do you transfer it to a different object or a different situation? We need to understand what prior structure helps, what can be learned from observing others, and what requires the robot's own trial and error.

And I would measure progress by generalization. Getting a robot to perform one carefully arranged demonstration is useful, but the deeper question is whether it has learned something that lets it cope when the circumstances change.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reusable skills and transfer, but does not describe increasingly complex skills as compositions of simpler ones.

r002.rationale: It gives a child’s example of handling an unfamiliar object, but does not explain that rapid complex-task learning can rely on skills acquired over many prior years.

r003.rationale: The response mentions prior structure and learning from experience, but does not identify making later robot-skill acquisition more efficient through previously acquired skills as a research goal.
